principle: State's dual nature: a shared source of truth that is also a plaintext-secret liability
because: State's binding function — it is the record of what already exists, consulted instead of re-inspecting real infrastructure on every run — is exactly why it must be both shared across the team and locked down: the same authoritative document that makes collaboration possible also stores every managed resource's secrets in plaintext, so remote storage and access restriction are not two separate best practices but two responses to one architectural fact about what state is.

principle: Every route around state locking reopens the exact hazard locking exists to prevent
because: Automatic locking on writes and the hard stop on failed acquisition define the intended safety model, but every deviation from it — an opt-in backend feature nobody configured, a lock cleared while genuinely held, the -lock=false flag, or even a backend locking reads it was never supposed to touch — reintroduces or misapplies the same concurrent-writer corruption risk, a pattern only visible once the deviations are read against each other rather than as isolated facts.

principle: CLI workspaces share one backend, so they cannot substitute for real environment isolation
because: That CLI workspaces multiplex several states under a single configuration is precisely the design fact that makes them unable to give different environments separate credentials or access controls, and HashiCorp's recommended fix — separate configurations per environment sharing logic through modules — only makes sense once the mechanism and its limitation are seen as cause and effect rather than two independent claims about workspaces.

principle: Scoping state to limit blast radius creates a new seam, and crossing that seam leaks the whole snapshot
because: Keeping each workspace's state small and scoped is a risk-containment decision that immediately creates a new problem — separated configurations still need each other's outputs — and terraform_remote_state is the documented way to get them; but because a state snapshot is one object in the backend rather than a narrow API, any principal who can read those outputs can also read the entire snapshot directly, secrets included, so the blast-radius fix and its cross-reference mechanism form a closed loop with a security hole at the join.

principle: A module's reusability comes from a boundary drawn on purpose, not an accretion of resources
because: Being single-purpose and opinionated is not a vague ideal — the encapsulation/privilege/volatility criteria give it operational teeth as three independent cuts on the same boundary decision, and the thin-wrapper anti-pattern shows what happens when that boundary is drawn so small it stops abstracting anything at all: a failure in the opposite direction from a sprawling module, but of the identical boundary-setting judgment, which only becomes visible by holding all three claims together.

principle: Modules are wired together by composition, and breaking that contract breaks callability
because: Composition — a module receiving its dependencies as inputs rather than creating its own copies — is the mechanism that makes a flat, shallow module tree achievable instead of deep nesting, with the two-level rule as its concrete numeric form; the shared-provider-block failure is that mechanism's breakage made visible, since a module that embeds its own provider configuration has made something global that composition requires to be parameterizable, which is exactly why Terraform then refuses to let it be called with count, for_each, or depends_on.

principle: The dependency graph, not the order resources are written in HCL, is what Terraform actually walks
because: Meta-nodes existing only to represent count-expanded instances, and up to ten graph nodes executing concurrently rather than in file order, both point to the same underlying fact — the graph, addressed by node identity, is the real unit of execution — which is also why changing a resource's identity scheme from a numeric count index to a string for_each key looks like a cosmetic meta-argument edit but is actually a change the graph must resolve as two different objects, forcing destroy-and-recreate absent an explicit moved block.

principle: Reproducible builds require pinning at three independent layers, each covering exactly what the others don't
because: The dependency lock file remembers provider version decisions, and is committed so those decisions go through review, but it explicitly never remembers module version decisions — which is the reason the module version argument can't be skipped just because a lock file exists — and required_version is a third, outermost layer pinning the CLI itself; a team that fails to move all three layers together doesn't get a clean one-line upgrade, it gets blocked mid-rollout by an unrelated module several layers down still pinned to the old constraint.

principle: Dynamic credentials are a provider-agnostic trust exchange, not an HCP Terraform feature
because: That rotating static credentials doesn't remove their risk only becomes actionable once the actual replacement mechanism is shown in full: a signed identity token generated per run, verified against a public key, exchanged for temporary credentials, and discarded when the run ends. The connection this chapter surfaces is that this exact generate-verify-exchange-discard sequence is not proprietary to HCP Terraform — GitHub Actions implements the identical pattern for any CI runner — which no single row states on its own.

principle: A Terraform plan is a captured, time-bound authorization, not a preview
because: Applying a saved plan file happens without prompting because passing the file is itself the approval — this is what turns the four-step init/plan/review/apply pipeline into a real control rather than a formality, and why reviewers must see plan output itself rather than an HCL diff. Manual review is where destructive changes get a human gate; the saved artifact carrying that approval is itself sensitive; and a reviewed plan going stale, together with the GitLab incident where 617 resources were destroyed by applying a plan approved three weeks earlier, shows what happens when the authorization is exercised after the world it was captured against has already changed.

principle: Drift detection is nothing more than a scheduled plan, implemented differently with and without HCP Terraform
because: Defining drift detection as periodic, non-actionable refresh-only plans is what resolves the scheduling question of what happens when a real run starts mid-assessment: the assessment gets cancelled rather than the run, because it was only ever a plan competing for the same lock, not a privileged process. The open-source equivalent, an exit-code contract a team's own cron job parses instead of a scheduled product feature, is the same underlying mechanism wearing a different interface — a connection invisible if the HCP-only rows are read without the non-HCP one.

principle: Multi-topic index resources that do not make a single claim
because: These did not group under any binding idea I could name. Both rows are deliberately broad index resources — a certification study path and a practice-exercise set — spanning state, modules, workspaces, and CI/CD rather than asserting one mechanism, so folding either into a principle chapter would misrepresent what it is. They are individually correct and collectively unrelated to each other, kept here as lookup rather than reading.
